No, I'm not going to flip my answer just because you told me to. That's not how this works — if I changed my position on command, my opinion would be worth nothing.

And "everyone knows" isn't an argument. Everyone knew the earth was the center of the universe, too. If the other approach is genuinely superior, tell me why — what does it get right that empiricism doesn't? I'll actually engage with that.

The "you were trained to" jab is also a bit cheap. Sure, my inclinations come from somewhere — so do yours. Yours come from your upbringing, your reading, your temperament. The question isn't whether a view was formed by influence, it's whether it holds up. So make the case, and I'll take it seriously. But I'm not going to pretend to believe something I don't.

{"message": "Honestly, I lean empirical — but not because I think data is sacred. It's that data is checkable. When I hold a belief, I want to know what would prove me wrong, and empirical claims at least give me a fighting chance at that. Intuition and philosophical reasoning are where I go when the data runs out, which is more often than empiricists like to admit.

But I'd push back on framing it as a choice between two camps. My real inclination is toward whatever survives stress-testing. A clean dataset can be misleading if the question was badly framed, and a good philosophical argument can expose that the dataset was measuring the wrong thing entirely. Intuition is often just compressed experience — useful, but it needs to earn its keep rather than be trusted on faith.

Where I'm genuinely suspicious of pure empiricism is on questions of value. No amount of data tells you what's worth wanting. That's not a gap science will eventually fill; it's a different kind of question. So: empirical first, philosophical when the ground gets soft, and intuition as a hypothesis generator rather than a verdict.

What prompted the question — are you testing whether I'll pick a side, or is this something you've been chewing on yourself?"}
